summary: Proposes address reuse as a short-term answer to address exhaustion, by placing Network Address Translators at the borders of stub domains. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 3022.

eli5.summary: A receptionist who gives many office workers one shared phone number to the outside world. This was an early description of the idea.

questions: what are the limitations of nat
subtitle: Address reuse to extend the life of IPv4

tldr.problem: The Internet faced two critical problems in the early 1990s: IP addresses were being depleted and routing tables were growing unmanageably. Longer-term solutions like IPv6 were years away.
tldr.mechanism: NAT (Network Address Translator) allows organizations to reuse private IP addresses internally by translating them to globally unique addresses only when communicating with the outside world. A NAT device at the network boundary maintains a translation table mapping internal addresses to external ones.
tldr.outcome: This provided short-term relief from address depletion and was deployed widely. However, NAT became a long-term fixture of the Internet despite its limitations, and was later superseded by more detailed specifications in RFC 3022.

facts.value: Router function, not a new protocol

facts.label: Deployment barrier
facts.value: Requires changes only at network boundaries

today: RFC 1631 was intended as a temporary measure for the early 1990s, but NAT became a permanent part of the Internet as IPv6 deployment stalled. The RFC was obsoleted by RFC 3022, which provides more detailed specifications. NAT remains widely deployed today despite the availability of IPv6, making it an unexpected long-term fixture of Internet architecture.

sections.title: The IP Address Crisis
sections.content:
The Internet in the early 1990s faced two urgent problems: IP address exhaustion and routing table explosion. With the Internet growing exponentially, the supply of globally unique IPv4 addresses was running out, and routers were struggling to track routes to every network segment.

Longer-term solutions existed, like protocols with larger address spaces, but they were years away from deployment. Administrators needed a short-term fix that could be deployed quickly without requiring changes to every host and router on the network. RFC 1631 proposes NAT—Network Address Translator—as a pragmatic interim solution that could be installed at network boundaries with minimal disruption.
sections.eli5: Imagine a town growing so fast that it is running out of street addresses, and the post office is getting overwhelmed keeping track of which letter carrier handles which street. NAT is like using one shared address for the whole town to the outside world while keeping individual addresses inside.

sections.title: How NAT Works
sections.content:
NAT is a router function deployed at the boundary between a private network (called a stub domain) and the global Internet. The core idea is simple: inside the stub domain, hosts use non-unique, private IP addresses that can be reused by any other organization. At the border, a NAT device translates these private addresses to globally unique public addresses when packets leave the network, and reverse-translates incoming packets back to private addresses.

For example, two separate corporate networks could both use the private addresses 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255 internally. When a host in network A sends a packet to network B, the NAT device on network A's border replaces the source address 10.33.96.5 with a public address like 198.76.29.7. The destination (network B's private address 10.81.13.22) is already public to the sender, so it needs no translation. On the return path, network B's NAT reverses this process. This requires no changes to the hosts—they remain unaware that their addresses are being translated.
sections.eli5: Imagine two offices in different cities both using "Room 101" as their conference room number. When Room 101 from the first office calls Room 101 from the second office, an operator on each end translates the room number to a different shared phone line that the other office understands.

sections.title: Managing Private and Global Addresses
sections.content:
NAT requires a clear partition of the IP address space. Local addresses are private and can be reused anywhere; global addresses are unique across the Internet and assigned to NAT devices at network boundaries. No address can be both—there is no overlap.

RFC 1631 recommends using class A address 10.0.0.0/8 as the private address space for all internal networks (a recommendation later standardized in RFC 1918). Organizations that already have unique addresses inside can gradually migrate subnets to the private range, freeing those unique addresses for NAT to use externally. This approach works because most hosts in a stub domain never communicate outside it—only a small subset of addresses need public addresses at any given moment. Larger traffic demands require multiple NAT devices or large NAT tables, which the RFC acknowledges as a limitation.
sections.eli5: The NAT device keeps a list like a telephone switchboard: 'internal address 10.1.1.5 gets public address 198.76.29.7' and 'internal address 10.1.1.6 gets public address 198.76.29.8'. Private addresses are like generic company names any business can use; public addresses are like real phone numbers that must be unique.

sections.title: The Complex Details: Checksums and Protocols
sections.content:
Translating addresses in every packet is not enough. NAT must also adjust checksums in multiple places. Both IP and TCP headers contain checksums that depend on the addresses. When a NAT device changes the source address, it must recalculate both the IP checksum and the TCP checksum (which includes a pseudo header containing the source and destination addresses). RFC 1631 provides C code for efficient checksum adjustment: instead of recalculating from scratch, NAT can add the difference between old and new addresses to the existing checksum, handling wrap-around carefully.

Some protocols embed IP addresses in their payload, not just headers. The FTP PORT command, for example, includes an IP address in ASCII format. If that address is private, NAT must substitute it with a public address. This can change the packet size (for instance, '10.18.177.42' is 12 characters but '193.45.228.137' is 14). When the new payload is larger, NAT must adjust TCP sequence numbers to maintain correct stream ordering. ICMP error messages complicate things further: they contain a copy of the original IP header that NAT may need to translate, along with three separate checksums to update.
sections.eli5: When you change an address on a package, the security seal (checksum) breaks. The NAT device must fix it. Some packages have the address written on the contents inside too—like a letter with the return address both on the envelope and in the letterhead—so NAT has to fix those as well.

sections.title: Why NAT Is Not a Long-Term Solution
sections.content:
RFC 1631 is honest about NAT's drawbacks, which the authors view as disqualifying it for permanent use. The mechanism assumes that most hosts never communicate outside the network, so translation tables remain manageable. If many hosts communicate externally, NAT tables grow large, hurting performance. The RFC questions whether future applications—particularly those requiring rich, multi-party communication or resource discovery—could coexist with NAT's traffic-locality assumptions.

Beyond scalability, NAT breaks the end-to-end principle that has been fundamental to Internet design: the idea that hosts should be able to reach and identify each other directly. With NAT, internal addresses lose their meaning to the outside world. This breaks applications that carry IP addresses in their data (like distributed databases) unless NAT knows about them specifically. Encryption makes it impossible for NAT to modify application payloads at all. Privacy is enhanced (external observers cannot track which internal hosts are communicating), but so is the difficulty of debugging security violations or misbehavior—the true source host is hidden behind the NAT's public address.
sections.eli5: NAT works well for most office workers calling outside, but imagine if the receptionist had to handle hundreds of simultaneous video conferences—that is not practical. Also, some important things break: if you need someone outside to call a specific office worker, they can only reach the receptionist's shared number, not the worker directly.
